title: Extending the Model
text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 3; Gupta et al. (2022).

title: Extending the Model
text:
The model
The monocentric city gives us a rent gradient. This week we ask how it changes when something in the economy changes: incomes rise, the population grows, or commuting gets cheaper. Economists call this comparative statics.

Two kinds of cities
The answer depends on whether people can move in and out.

In a closed city, the population is fixed. A change shows up in residents’ well-being (their consumption \(c\)) and in rents.
In an open city, people move freely, so residents always end up exactly as well off as they could be elsewhere. A change shows up in population and city size, and landowners collect the gains or bear the losses.



What happens when commuting gets cheaper
With fixed lot sizes, rent at distance \(x\) is \(r(x) = r_A + t(\bar{x} - x)\). Lower \(t\), and:

Closed city: the edge \(\bar{x}\) stays put (same people, same lots), the rent line flattens, and rent falls everywhere inside the edge. Residents keep the savings.
Open city: residents’ well-being is pinned by the outside option, so CBD rent stays at \(y - \bar{c}\). The flatter line reaches farmland farther out, so the city expands and newcomers move in.

In Brueckner’s full model, where households also choose how much space to use, cheaper commuting lets people spread out even in a closed city: rents fall near the center and rise toward the edge, and the city grows outward.


Remote work as a fall in \(t\)
If you commute only on the days you go to the office, working from home some days cuts your yearly commuting cost. With \(d\) remote days in a five-day week, the effective commuting cost becomes
\[
t_{\text{eff}} = t \left(1 - \frac{d}{5}\right).
\]
So the model predicts that remote work flattens the rent gradient: central locations lose some of their premium relative to outlying ones.

title: Extending the Model
Extending the Model
text:
What the evidence says
Gupta et al. (2022) study U.S. housing markets during the pandemic. They find that house prices and rents fell in city centers relative to the suburbs in large metro areas, so the gradient of prices with distance from the center flattened, and the effect was larger where more jobs could be done remotely. That is exactly the comparative static in the simulation: a lower effective \(t\) flattens the gradient. Whether the flattening lasts depends on how much remote work sticks.

title: Extending the Model
text:
Closer to home

During the pandemic, many remote workers moved to Maine from Boston and New York. In open-city terms, what happened to the “outside option” that Maine towns compete with?
If a Portland worker goes to the office two days a week instead of five, how much farther out could they live for the same total commuting cost?


Network lens: rail networks and the first commuters
The same comparative static played out 150 years ago, along a network of rail lines. Heblich et al. (2020) study London in the nineteenth century. As steam railways spread, commuting got much cheaper, and people could live and work in different places for the first time on a large scale. Residents spread outward along the rail network while jobs concentrated in the center, a lower \(t\) along the links of a network rather than in every direction at once.

title: Extending the Model
text:
Did you know?
Before streetcars and railways, most city residents lived within walking distance of their jobs, and historians call those places “walking cities.” Horse-drawn and then electric streetcars in the late nineteenth century lowered \(t\) and produced the first streetcar suburbs, decades before the automobile.

title: Why Cities Exist
text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 1; Glaeser (1998); Glaeser and Gottlieb (2009); Bailey et al. (2018).

title: Why Cities Exist
text:
The model
Rent for a one-bedroom apartment in Boston is far higher than in rural Maine. Commutes are longer, streets are louder, and parking is scarce. Yet roughly four in five Americans live in urban areas. Why do so many people pay more to live close to one another? Because being close to other people and firms makes us more productive and gives us access to things we value.

Why not spread out?
In a world where everyone could produce what they need on their own plot, with no advantage to working at scale, there would be no reason to live near anyone, and land would be cheap everywhere. Cities appear because of two forces:

Scale economies. Some goods are much cheaper to make in large plants or offices, so production concentrates in a few places and workers live nearby.
Transport costs. Moving goods, people, and ideas takes money and time, so it pays to locate near customers, suppliers, ports, and rivers.



Agglomeration economies
Once a city exists, firms become more productive simply because other firms and workers are nearby. These agglomeration economies work through three channels (Duranton and Puga 2004):

Sharing: firms share suppliers, infrastructure, and a large pool of workers.
Matching: a big labor market makes it easier to fit the right worker to each job.
Learning: ideas spread faster when people meet face to face.

Localization economies come from many firms in the same industry clustering together; urbanization economies come from the size and variety of the whole city.


Spatial equilibrium across cities
If big cities make workers more productive, why doesn’t everyone move to the highest-wage city? Because moving bids the advantage away. A worker in city \(i\) earns wage \(w_i\), pays rent \(r_i\), and enjoys amenities worth \(a_i\):
\[
V_i = w_i - r_i + a_i = \bar{V} \quad \text{for every city } i.
\]
With free mobility, utility is the same everywhere for the marginal mover (Roback 1982; Glaeser and Gottlieb 2009). High wages with high rents signal a productive city; high rents with low wages signal valuable amenities.


How big does a city get?
Agglomeration benefits grow with population, but so do congestion and housing costs. So utility per resident first rises with population, peaks at some size \(N^*\), and then falls. People move in as long as the city beats the utility \(\bar{u}\) they could get elsewhere. The simulation shows where that leaves the city.

title: Why Cities Exist
text:
Simulation
Utility per resident is \(u(N) = 20 + aN - cN^2\), where \(a\) measures agglomeration benefits and \(c\) congestion costs. Population \(N\) is in hundreds of thousands.



Show the simulation code
viewof aggl = Inputs.range([2, 14], {value: 8, step: 0.5, label: "Agglomeration benefit, a"})
viewof cong = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {value: 0.8, step: 0.05, label: "Congestion cost, c"})
viewof ubar = Inputs.range([10, 50], {value: 30, step: 0.5, label: "Utility available elsewhere, ū"})

})

The left-hand crossing is unstable. Explain why a few extra residents there would set off a rush of growth.

title: Why Cities Exist
text:
What the evidence says
Are cities dying? In the 1990s many observers expected cheaper phone calls and the internet to make cities obsolete. Glaeser (1998) argued that cities exist to cut the cost of moving goods, people, and ideas. Cheaper shipping weakened the first reason, but face-to-face learning and urban amenities kept cities alive. The same debate came back with remote work after COVID-19 (Extending the Model).
Do cities make workers more productive? Glaeser and Gottlieb (2009) show that wages are higher in larger, denser metro areas, but so are housing costs, which absorb much of the gain, just as spatial equilibrium predicts. A hard question is whether big cities make workers more productive or simply attract more productive workers; separating the two is a recurring challenge in urban economics.

title: Why Cities Exist
text:
Closer to home
Lewiston grew around the falls of the Androscoggin River, whose water power ran large textile mills. Mills needed many workers, and workers needed housing and stores within walking distance: a city built on scale economies. When the textile industry moved away in the twentieth century, Lewiston lost jobs and population. In the early 2000s, immigrants and refugees, many from Somalia, began arriving and opening businesses downtown, and parts of the old mill complex have been redeveloped for offices, restaurants, and housing.

Water power no longer matters. What advantages does Lewiston–Auburn have today?
Portland has grown faster than Lewiston–Auburn. Is that because of productivity, amenities, or both? What data would tell them apart?


Network lens: proximity still shapes who knows whom
The learning channel of agglomeration is a claim about networks: ideas travel along personal connections, and connections form more easily between people who are close together. Bailey et al. (2018) measure this with the Social Connectedness Index, built from anonymized Facebook friendships between U.S. counties:
\[
\text{SCI}_{ij} = \frac{\text{friendship links between } i \text{ and } j}{\text{users in } i \times \text{users in } j}.
\]
Even on a global social network, friendships fall off steeply with distance, counties in the same state are more connected than equally distant counties across state lines, and more-connected places trade more and exchange more migrants. Distance still matters, which is one reason the learning benefits of cities persist.



Illustrative shape of distance decay in social connectedness (simulated data; see Bailey et al. 2018 for the real estimates).


The SCI data are public through Meta’s Data for Good program. Try listing the counties most connected to Androscoggin County, Maine, and compare them with Cumberland County.

title: Why Cities Exist
text:
Did you know?
Bates College takes its name from Benjamin Bates, the Boston investor behind the Bates Manufacturing Company, whose mills on the Androscoggin made Lewiston one of Maine’s major industrial cities. The college sits a short walk from the mills that once paid for it.

title: The Monocentric City
text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 2; Rosenthal et al. (2022).

title: The Monocentric City
text:
The model
Picture a city where every job is downtown, in the central business district (CBD). Everyone earns the same income and commutes to the CBD. Living farther out means a longer, more expensive commute. So why would anyone live far away? Because housing is cheaper there. This trade-off between commuting cost and housing cost is the heart of the Alonso–Muth–Mills model.

The rent gradient
Keep it simple: every household lives on one lot of the same size. A household at distance \(x\) miles from the CBD earns income \(y\), pays rent \(r(x)\) for its lot, pays commuting cost \(t\) per mile per year, and spends what is left, \(c\), on everything else:
\[
c = y - t\,x - r(x).
\]
If households could be better off at one location than another, they would move there and bid up its rent. So in equilibrium, everyone gets the same \(c\), wherever they live. Rearranging:
\[
r(x) = y - t\,x - c.
\]
Rent falls by exactly \(t\) for every extra mile. Being one mile closer to the CBD saves \(t\) in commuting, and landlords capture that saving in rent. The downward-sloping line is the rent gradient.


The edge of the city
The city stops where urban rent falls to what the land would earn in farming, the agricultural rent \(r_A\). Call that distance \(\bar{x}\). If the city has \(N\) households and \(D\) lots per square mile, it fills a circle of area \(\pi \bar{x}^2\), so
\[
\bar{x} = \sqrt{\frac{N}{\pi D}}, \qquad r(x) = r_A + t\,(\bar{x} - x).
\]
Rent at the CBD is \(r_A + t\bar{x}\): agricultural rent plus the commuting cost saved by living downtown instead of at the edge.


Closed and open cities

In a closed city, the population \(N\) is fixed. Changes show up in residents’ consumption \(c\).
In an open city, people can move in or out freely, so \(c\) is pinned to what they could get elsewhere. Changes show up in population and in the city’s size.

The full Brueckner model also lets households choose how much space to use. Then dwellings are smaller and buildings taller near the CBD, and the rent curve bends instead of being a straight line. The fixed-lot version here keeps the arithmetic simple while preserving the key logic.

title: The Monocentric City
The Monocentric City
text:
What the evidence says
The model’s central prediction, that land and housing are most expensive near the center and cheaper farther out, holds in most cities. The interesting questions are how steep the gradient is and how it changes.
Rosenthal et al. (2022) ask whether COVID-19 made city centers less valuable for businesses. Using commercial real estate rents, they find that the rent premium for dense, central locations fell after the pandemic began, especially in cities where many workers commute by public transit. In model terms, the value of being close to the center declined. Whether that change is permanent is still an open question, and we return to it with remote work in Extending the Model.

title: The Monocentric City
text:
Closer to home
Portland’s peninsula is the closest thing in Maine to a classic CBD: offices, the port, and many restaurants are packed into a small area, and the Casco Bay coastline limits how far the center can spread.

If you looked up rents on the peninsula and in towns at increasing distance (South Portland, Westbrook, Gorham, and beyond), would you expect a clean gradient? What else besides commuting distance might affect rents?
Lewiston–Auburn has two downtowns facing each other across the Androscoggin River. How well does a single-center model describe it?


Network lens: where you live shapes where you work
The model treats the commute as a cost of distance. But location also determines who your neighbors are, and neighbors pass along job leads. Using Boston-area census data, Bayer et al. (2008) compare people living on the same city block with people living on nearby blocks in the same small area. People on the same block are more likely to work at the same place, consistent with informal job referrals among neighbors. A residential location is not just a point on a rent gradient; it is also a position in a social network.

title: The Monocentric City
text:
Did you know?
The rent gradient is older than the city model. In 1826 the German economist Johann Heinrich von Thünen showed that farmland closer to a market town earns higher rent because crops cost less to haul there. William Alonso adapted the idea to households commuting to downtown jobs in his 1964 book Location and Land Use, and Richard Muth and Edwin Mills developed it further. That is why the model carries their three names.

title: Owning versus Renting
text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 6; Painter et al. (2001).

title: Owning versus Renting
text:
The model
Should you buy a home or rent one? The sticker price of a house is the wrong comparison. What matters is the annual cost of owning, called the user cost, compared with a year’s rent for a similar home.

The user cost of owning
Owning a home worth \(V\) for a year costs you:

Interest on the money tied up in the home, \(iV\), whether it is paid to a bank on a mortgage or forgone on your own savings;
Property tax, \(pV\);
Maintenance and depreciation, \(dV\);

minus

Expected appreciation, \(gV\), the gain if the home’s value rises.

Without taxes, the user cost is \((i + p + d - g)V\).


Where the tax code comes in
The U.S. income tax treats owners and renters differently. A landlord pays income tax on rent received; an owner-occupier pays no tax on the housing services they “rent to themselves.” Owners who itemize can also deduct mortgage interest and property taxes. For a household with marginal tax rate \(\tau\) that itemizes,
\[
\text{user cost} = \big[(1 - \tau)(i + p) + d - g\big] V.
\]
The deductions are worth more to households in higher tax brackets, so higher-income households face a lower cost of owning and are more likely to own. Households that expect to move soon tend to rent, because buying and selling a home is expensive.

What the evidence says
Homeownership rates differ widely across groups. Painter et al. (2001) use household data from Los Angeles to ask how much of the gaps across racial, ethnic, and immigrant groups can be explained by differences in income, household characteristics, and, for immigrants, how long they have lived in the United States. Network lens: your friends’ housing markets
Expected appreciation \(g\) is a belief, and beliefs spread through social networks. Bailey et al. (2018) link Facebook friendship networks to housing transactions for Los Angeles residents. People whose friends in other cities had recently seen bigger house-price gains were more likely to buy rather than rent, bought larger homes, and paid more. Because friends live in many different housing markets, these experiences vary for reasons unrelated to the buyer’s own neighborhood, which helps the authors separate the effect of friends’ experiences from local conditions. title: Pollution and Crime
text:
The model
Cities put people close together, which makes both pollution and crime more costly. Both topics turn on externalities and on how people respond to incentives.

Pollution: Pigou and Coase
A factory that ignores the harm its emissions cause to neighbors produces where price equals its marginal private cost. The efficient output sets price equal to marginal social cost, private cost plus the marginal damage to others:
\[
P = MPC(Q) + MD(Q).
\]
A Pigouvian tax equal to marginal damage at the efficient output makes the factory face the full cost. The Coase theorem offers another route: if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the factory and its neighbors can negotiate to the efficient outcome on their own. In a dense city with thousands of affected residents, bargaining is rarely cheap.


Crime: incentives and social interactions
In Gary Becker’s model, a person commits a crime when the benefit exceeds the expected cost: the probability of being caught, \(p\), times the punishment, \(f\). Raising either deters crime, but the evidence favors certainty over severity.
People also respond to one another. If each person’s behavior depends partly on what their peers do, a policy that directly reduces crime by some amount sets off a chain of further reductions. With individual crime rate \(a = b + s\,\bar{a}\), where \(b\) reflects a person’s own incentives, \(\bar{a}\) the average among peers, and \(0 < s < 1\) the strength of peer effects, the equilibrium is
\[
a = \frac{b}{1 - s}.
\]
The factor \(1/(1-s)\) is the social multiplier.

title: Pollution and Crime
text:
What the evidence says
What people pay to avoid pollution. Currie et al. (2015) study about 1,600 openings and closings of industrial plants that emit toxic pollutants. Comparing homes very close to a plant with homes slightly farther away, before and after, they find that nearby home values fall when a plant opens and recover after it closes, and that infants born close to plants are in worse health. House prices reveal what people are willing to pay for cleaner air, the hedonic approach.
What deters crime. Chalfin and McCrary (2017) review the evidence and conclude that increases in the certainty of being caught, especially through more police, reduce crime more reliably than increases in the severity of punishment, such as longer sentences. Offenders may weigh the immediate risk of arrest more than a distant prison term.

text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 5; Duranton and Turner (2011); Tarduno (2021).

title: Traffic Congestion
text:
The model
Every driver who enters a crowded highway slows down everyone else a little. No single driver notices the few seconds they add to each other car’s trip, but across thousands of cars those seconds add up. That ignored cost is a classic externality, and it is why rush-hour traffic is worse than it should be.

Average cost versus marginal cost
Let \(T\) be the number of cars per hour. The cost of a trip to each driver, time plus operating cost, rises with traffic:
\[
AC(T) = a + bT.
\]
The total cost of all trips is \(T \cdot AC(T) = aT + bT^2\), so the marginal social cost of one more car is
\[
MC(T) = a + 2bT.
\]
The gap, \(MC - AC = bT\), is the delay the extra car imposes on everyone else.


Two equilibria
Drivers’ willingness to pay for a trip is the demand curve, \(MB(T) = \alpha - \beta T\).

Without a toll, drivers keep entering until the benefit of the last trip equals the cost they pay: \(MB = AC\). Too many people drive.
The efficient level sets benefit equal to the full social cost: \(MB = MC\).

A congestion toll equal to \(bT^*\), the external cost at the efficient level of traffic, closes the gap. Drivers then face \(AC + \text{toll} = MC\), and traffic falls to \(T^*\). The deadweight loss of having no toll is the triangle between \(MC\) and \(MB\) from \(T^*\) to the unpriced level of traffic.

title: Traffic Congestion
text:
What the evidence says
New lanes fill up. Duranton and Turner (2011) find that vehicle-kilometers traveled in U.S. metro areas rise roughly one-for-one with lane-kilometers of interstate highway. When capacity grows, residents drive more, trucks and businesses use the roads more, and people move in. In the simulation, adding capacity lowers the cost curves, and traffic grows along the demand curve. The more elastic demand is, the more the new capacity fills up and the less travel times improve.
Ride-hailing adds traffic. Tarduno (2021) uses the temporary exit of Uber and Lyft from Austin, Texas, in 2016 as a natural experiment and finds that traffic volumes fell after they left. Ride-hailing trips impose the same unpriced delay on other drivers as any other car.
The policy lesson from both papers: pricing the road changes behavior; adding capacity alone mostly invites more driving.

title: Traffic Congestion
text:
Closer to home
Maine’s congestion is modest by big-city standards, but it is concentrated: Portland’s peninsula at rush hour, the bridges between Lewiston and Auburn, and the Maine Turnpike on summer weekends.

The Maine Turnpike already charges tolls. Are they congestion tolls? What would a congestion toll on a summer Friday afternoon look like?
Suppose Lewiston proposes widening a busy downtown street. Using the fundamental law, what would you expect to happen to traffic two or three years later?


Network lens: roads are a network, not a single road
The model above looks at one road. Real trips run through a network of roads, and drivers switch routes when one gets crowded. Widening one road pulls traffic away from others, so part of the benefit shows up elsewhere in the network, and part disappears as the widened road fills up. Allen and Arkolakis (2022) build a model of route choice on the U.S. interstate system and on Seattle’s roads and find that the returns to improving individual road segments vary widely; accounting for congestion and rerouting changes which projects look best. A famous network puzzle, Braess’s paradox, shows that adding a road can even make everyone’s trip slower.

title: Traffic Congestion
text:
Did you know?
Economist William Vickrey argued for road pricing beginning in the 1950s and 1960s, and later shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in economics. His ideas took decades to reach the street. Singapore began charging drivers to enter its downtown in 1975. London introduced a congestion charge in 2003, and Stockholm adopted one permanently in 2007 after a trial. In January 2025, New York City became the first U.S. city to charge drivers to enter its central business district.

title: Sprawl and Land-Use Controls
text:
The model
Cities grow outward because, at the edge, land is worth more to a developer than to a farmer. That is efficient if prices reflect all costs and benefits. Brueckner identifies three market failures that make the market edge too far out:

Unvalued open space. Farmland and woods at the fringe give nearby residents views, recreation, and habitat. The farmer’s rent \(r_A\) leaves this out, so land is converted too cheaply.
Unpriced congestion. Drivers do not pay for the delay they impose on others (Traffic Congestion). Commuting feels cheaper than it really is, so people live too far out.
Unpaid infrastructure costs. New subdivisions often pay the average cost of roads, pipes, and schools rather than the higher marginal cost of serving the fringe.


Market edge versus efficient edge
Take an open city where residents earn \(y\), enjoy consumption \(\bar{c}\) set by the outside option, and pay commuting cost \(t\) per mile. Urban land at distance \(x\) rents for \(r(x) = y - \bar{c} - t x\), and the market city stops where this falls to \(r_A\):
\[
\bar{x}_{\text{market}} = \frac{y - \bar{c} - r_A}{t}.
\]
Now count the social costs: each mile of commuting also imposes a congestion cost \(e\) on others, and each lot of farmland has an open-space value \(v\). The efficient edge is where the social value of urban land equals the social value of farmland:
\[
\bar{x}_{\text{efficient}} = \frac{y - \bar{c} - r_A - v}{t + e}.
\]
Both corrections pull the efficient edge inward. The gap is excess sprawl.


Fixing it
The best remedy targets the failure directly: a congestion toll for unpriced driving, an open-space or development tax (or public purchase of land) for lost open space, and impact fees for infrastructure. A blunter tool is an urban growth boundary, which caps the edge directly but does not distinguish among the reasons for sprawl.

text:
What the evidence says
Critics of sprawl often point to health: people in sprawling neighborhoods drive more, walk less, and are heavier on average. Eid et al. (2008) ask whether sprawl causes weight gain or whether people who are already prone to it choose sprawling neighborhoods. Following the same individuals over time as they move between more and less sprawling places, they find no evidence that sprawl causes weight gain; the correlation reflects sorting. The lesson for policy: the case against sprawl rests on the market failures above, not on health.

title: Sprawl and Land-Use Controls
text:
Closer to home

Maine’s 1988 Growth Management Act encourages towns to plan for designated growth areas. Which of the three market failures does growth-area planning address?
Picture new subdivisions along the roads out of Lewiston–Auburn or Portland. Who pays for the new roads, school buses, and water lines?


Network lens: highways as spokes of a network
Sprawl follows the transportation network. Baum-Snow (2007) asks how much of postwar suburbanization was caused by the interstate highway system. Because highways were not built at random, he uses the 1947 national highway plan to predict where highway “rays” would run through central cities. He finds that each additional ray reduced central-city population by roughly 18 percent. In the model, a new highway is a lower \(t\) along one spoke of the network, and the city stretches out along it.

title: Sprawl and Land-Use Controls
text:
Did you know?
Oregon’s 1973 land-use law required its cities to draw urban growth boundaries, and the Portland, Oregon, metro area adopted its boundary in 1979. It remains the best-known growth boundary in the United States and a common case study in debates over whether boundaries raise housing prices.

title: Housing Policy
text: Read: Brueckner, Chapter 7; Ellen (2020); Diamond et al. (2019).

title: Housing Policy
text:
The model
Governments help renters in two main ways: by limiting rents and by paying part of the rent. Simple economics gives sharp predictions about both, and recent research adds important nuance.

Rent control
A rent ceiling below the market rent has three effects in the basic supply-and-demand model:

A shortage. At the lower rent, more people want apartments and landlords offer fewer.
A transfer. Tenants who keep a controlled apartment pay less; that money comes out of landlords’ pockets.
A deadweight loss. Apartments that renters value more than they cost to supply are no longer offered.

Because price no longer rations apartments, something else does: waiting lists, connections, or lower maintenance. Tenants also stay put longer, since leaving means losing the controlled rent.


Vouchers versus public housing
A housing voucher pays part of a family’s rent in a private apartment of their choosing. Public housing offers a specific unit. In a budget-constraint diagram, a voucher shifts the budget line out, while public housing offers one fixed bundle on that same line. So a family is at least as well off with a voucher of equal cost, and usually better off, because it can choose. Governments may still prefer in-kind help to make sure aid is spent on housing or to add housing where it is scarce.

title: Housing Policy
text:
Simulation
Quantity is in thousands of apartments, rent in dollars per month. The starting values match Problem B1 on Midterm 2.



Show the simulation code
viewof ceiling = Inputs.range([500, 1200], {value: 800, step: 10, label: "Rent ceiling ($ per month)"})
viewof dInt = Inputs.range([60, 140], {value: 100, step: 1, label: "Demand: Qd = intercept − 0.04 P. Intercept"})

title: Housing Policy
text:
What the evidence says
Rent control in San Francisco. In 1994, San Francisco extended rent control to small multifamily buildings built before 1980, while similar buildings built after 1980 stayed uncontrolled. Diamond et al. (2019) compare the two groups. Tenants in newly covered buildings were much more likely to stay in their homes and in the city, a real benefit the simple model misses. But landlords of covered buildings cut the supply of rental housing by about 15 percent, by converting units to condominiums, moving in themselves, or redeveloping. Less rental housing pushed up rents for everyone else.
Housing vouchers. Ellen (2020) reviews what we know about the Housing Choice Voucher program. Vouchers reduce homelessness, crowding, and rent burdens. But many voucher holders still live in relatively poor neighborhoods, and only a fraction of eligible families receive a voucher at all. Reforms that help families reach a wider range of neighborhoods are an active area of policy.

title: Housing Policy
text:
Closer to home

In 2020, Portland voters approved a rent control ordinance that limits annual rent increases for many apartments. Using the simulation and the San Francisco evidence, what would you predict for Portland’s rental supply over the next decade? What would you want to measure?
Lewiston has many older multifamily buildings. Would a voucher or rent control do more for low-income renters there? Why?


Network lens: vouchers and social ties
Where a voucher gets used depends on more than rent and housing quality. Families often look for apartments near relatives and friends who help with childcare, transportation, and job leads, and landlords often fill units through word of mouth. A voucher that technically allows a move to a high-opportunity neighborhood may go unused if a family’s support network lives elsewhere. Thinking of housing search as moving within a social network helps explain why mobility counseling and landlord outreach can matter as much as the dollar value of the subsidy.

title: Housing Policy
text:
Did you know?
The Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck famously quipped that, short of bombing, rent control may be the most efficient way to destroy a city. Economists still largely agree on the supply effects, but the San Francisco evidence shows why the debate continues: rent control also protects incumbent tenants from displacement.

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
The model
Some policies help people wherever they live: tax credits, job training, health insurance. Others help places: tax breaks for firms that locate in a struggling town, infrastructure grants, enterprise zones. Place-based policies are popular with politicians but controversial among economists. Why?

The case against: benefits get capitalized
In a spatial equilibrium, people move until no place is better than another. If a policy makes a town more attractive, newcomers arrive and bid up rents. When people move easily and housing is hard to build, much of the gain ends up in landowners’ pockets rather than with the workers the policy meant to help. Subsidizing places can also pull jobs from one town to another without creating any new jobs overall.


The case for: local multipliers and non-employment
Two arguments push the other way.

Local multipliers. A new job in a tradable industry, one that sells outside the town, such as manufacturing or software, brings income into the local economy. That income supports additional non-tradable jobs: restaurants, stores, contractors, dentists. If each new tradable job supports \(m\) local jobs, the total job gain is

\[
\text{total jobs} = J\,(1 + m).
\]

Where jobs matter most. If places differ in how much jobs reduce non-employment and its harms, then putting jobs where the response is largest can raise overall well-being. This is the core argument in Austin et al. (2018).

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
Simulation
A state offers a subsidy to attract new tradable jobs to a town. How many jobs does it create in total, and what does each job cost?



Show the simulation code

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
What the evidence says
Local multipliers. Moretti (2010) estimates how many local jobs follow each new tradable job across U.S. cities. He finds that each additional manufacturing job is associated with about 1.6 additional jobs in the local non-tradable sector, and that the multiplier is larger for skilled and high-tech jobs.
Jobs for the heartland. Austin et al. (2018) document that non-employment among prime-age men has become concentrated in parts of the eastern United States and argue that place-based policies can be justified where employment responds most strongly to policy. They favor policies that encourage employment, such as targeted employment subsidies, over policies that simply move jobs between places.

title: Place-Based Policy
text:
Closer to home

Lewiston–Auburn and many mill towns lost tradable manufacturing jobs over the past century. Using the multiplier logic, what happened to local service jobs when the mills closed?
Maine uses tax incentives to attract and keep businesses. Pick one program and ask: how many of the subsidized jobs would have come anyway?


Network lens: towns are nodes in a regional network
Lewiston–Auburn is linked to Portland by commuters, freight, and social ties. A job created in Portland can raise employment in Lewiston–Auburn through commuting, and a subsidy in one town can draw workers and businesses from its neighbors. Treating towns as nodes in a regional network, rather than islands, helps answer two questions that place-based policy often ignores: who actually fills the new jobs, and how much of the gain spills over to, or is taken from, nearby places.

Economists still study it to learn whether a large, temporary push can permanently change a region’s economy.

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text: Read: Glaeser and Gyourko (2018); Saiz (2010).

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text:
The model
When more people want to live in a city, two things can happen: builders add homes, or prices rise. Which one wins depends on the price elasticity of housing supply, \(\varepsilon_S\): the percentage increase in the housing stock when prices rise 1 percent.

Supply, demand, and elasticities
With constant-elasticity supply and demand, if demand rises by \(X\) percent (at every price, people want \(X\) percent more housing), the new equilibrium satisfies
\[
\%\Delta P \approx \frac{X}{\varepsilon_S + \varepsilon_D}, \qquad \%\Delta Q \approx \varepsilon_S \cdot \%\Delta P,
\]
where \(\varepsilon_D\) is the (absolute) price elasticity of demand. When supply is elastic, the boom shows up mostly as new homes. When supply is inelastic, it shows up mostly as higher prices.


What makes supply inelastic?

Geography. Water, wetlands, and steep slopes leave less land to build on.
Regulation. Zoning, minimum lot sizes, height limits, parking requirements, and slow permitting raise the cost of adding homes.



Prices versus construction costs
A useful test: compare home prices with the minimum profitable production cost, what it costs to build a home plus a normal profit and a modest amount of land. If prices sit far above that cost for years, something is preventing builders from adding homes, which economists often interpret as an implicit “regulatory tax.”

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text:
Simulation
Prices and quantities start at 100 (index values). Increase demand and see how the outcome depends on supply elasticity.



Show the simulation code

viewof eS = Inputs.range([0.1, 5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Supply elasticity, εS"})
viewof eD = Inputs.range([0.2, 1.5], {value: 0.7, step: 0.05, label: "Demand elasticity, εD (absolute value)"})

























Show the simulation code

Q1 = 100 * Math.pow(P1 / 100, eS)
Pgrid = d3.range(60, 200, 1)
Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Housing quantity (index) →", domain: [60, 200]},
  y: {label: "↑ Price (index)", domain: [60, 200], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Supply", "Demand before", "Demand after"], range: ["#2b6cb0", "#999", "#881124"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(Pgrid, {x: p => 100 * Math.pow(p / 100, eS), y: p => p, stroke: () => "Supply", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line(Pgrid, {x: p => 100 * Math.pow(p / 100, -eD), y: p => p, stroke: () => "Demand before", strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
    Plot.line(Pgrid, {x: p => 100 * (1 + X / 100) * Math.pow(p / 100, -eD), y: p => p, stroke: () => "Demand after", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{q: 100, p: 100}, {q: Q1, p: P1}], {x: "q", y: "p", r: 5, fill: "black"})
  ]
})

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text:
What the evidence says
Geography and regulation together. Saiz (2010) measures how much land within reach of each U.S. metro area’s center is lost to water and steep slopes, using satellite and elevation data. Metros with more unbuildable land have less elastic housing supply, and those same metros also tend to have stricter land-use regulation. Supply elasticity, in turn, shapes whether demand growth shows up as price growth or as new homes.
Prices far above building costs. Glaeser and Gyourko (2018) compare home prices with the minimum profitable production cost. In most of the United States, prices are close to that cost. In a set of high-demand, mostly coastal metros, they are far above it, which points to regulation rather than construction costs as the main reason housing is expensive there. They also argue that restrictions in productive cities keep workers out of the places where they would earn the most.

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text:
Closer to home

Portland, Maine, sits on a peninsula, with Casco Bay and Back Cove limiting buildable land near downtown. Which part of Saiz’s measure does that resemble?
Maine passed a 2022 law that requires towns to allow more types of housing, such as accessory dwelling units, in many areas. In the simulation, what would that do to \(\varepsilon_S\), and what would you expect to happen to prices?


Network lens: housing markets are linked by commutes
A city’s housing market is not an island. Commuting networks tie Portland to South Portland, Westbrook, Scarborough, and towns farther out, and tie Lewiston–Auburn to Portland and Augusta. When building is constrained in the center, demand spills along the commuting links into surrounding towns, raising prices there and lengthening commutes. Mapping commuting flows (for example, from Census commuting data) shows which towns are part of the same housing market and where new housing would relieve the most pressure.

title: Housing Supply and Affordability
text:
Did you know?
The idea that land-use regulation acts like a tax on new housing goes back decades, but Glaeser and Gyourko’s comparison of prices with construction costs made it measurable for every metro area, and it now shapes debates over zoning reform across the country.

title: Local Public Goods and Neighborhoods
text:
The model
Schools, parks, police, and trash pickup are mostly provided by local governments and paid for with local property taxes. Because people can choose where to live, they can also choose their package of public services and taxes.

Tiebout sorting
Charles Tiebout argued that when there are many towns, households “vote with their feet,” sorting into the town whose mix of services and taxes best matches what they want. With enough towns, this can provide local public goods efficiently, something a single national government struggles to do because it cannot easily learn how much each person values them.
The argument needs strong assumptions: many towns to choose among, people who can move easily, no spillovers between towns, and taxes that work like a price for services. Property taxes break the last assumption: a family in a small house pays less tax than a neighbor in a large house but uses the same schools. Zoning, such as minimum lot sizes, keeps out lower-tax households and restores the link between taxes and services, but at the cost of excluding families with less income.


Capitalization
If a town’s schools are better or its taxes are lower, families bid more for homes there. The advantage gets built into house prices. If a home comes with a benefit worth \(B\) dollars per year forever, and buyers discount the future at interest rate \(r\), the price premium is
\[
\Delta P = \frac{B}{r}.
\]
Capitalization means that whoever owns the home when the improvement is announced collects the gain. Later buyers pay for the better schools in the price.

title: Local Public Goods and Neighborhoods
text:
What the evidence says
Paying to live in a richer town. Boustan (2013) compares homes on either side of municipal borders, where neighborhoods look similar but the town differs. Homes on the side of a higher-income town sell for more. She asks how much of that premium reflects local public goods and fiscal advantages, a direct test of Tiebout-style sorting and capitalization.
Do neighborhoods change children’s futures? In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, families in high-poverty public housing were randomly offered housing vouchers, some of which could be used only in low-poverty neighborhoods. Chetty et al. (2016) follow the children into adulthood. Children who moved to lower-poverty neighborhoods when young, before about age 13, had higher earnings and college attendance as adults; those who moved as teenagers did not benefit. The longer a child spends in a better neighborhood, the larger the gain. Because the offers were random, these are causal effects of place.

title: Local Public Goods and Neighborhoods
text:
Closer to home

Maine funds schools through a mix of local property taxes and state aid. Look up the school budgets and tax rates of Lewiston, Auburn, and a nearby suburb. What would Tiebout predict about who lives where?
Two Maine towns with similar homes have different school ratings. How would you use home sale prices to estimate what families pay for the difference?


Network lens: who you know, not just where you live
Neighborhoods matter partly because of the social networks they create. Chetty et al. (2022) use billions of Facebook friendships to measure economic connectedness: how many higher-income friends people with lower incomes have. Across U.S. counties and ZIP codes, economic connectedness is the strongest predictor of upward mobility among the social-capital measures they study. These are associations, not causal estimates, but they suggest that part of what Moving to Opportunity changed was the networks children grew up in.

title: Local Public Goods and Neighborhoods
text:
Did you know?
Charles Tiebout’s 1956 paper was a reply to Paul Samuelson, who had argued in 1954 that markets cannot reveal how much people value public goods. Tiebout’s answer, that moving between towns can reveal those values, became one of the most cited ideas in public and urban economics.

title: Measuring Quality of Life
text:
The model
How do you put a dollar value on sunshine, a coastline, or low crime? You can’t buy them directly, but you can see what people give up to have them. That is the idea behind quality-of-life rankings in urban economics.

Reading amenities from prices
Return to spatial equilibrium across cities (Why Cities Exist). If workers can move freely, then in every city
\[
w_i - r_i + a_i = \bar{V},
\]
where \(w_i\) is the wage, \(r_i\) the cost of housing, and \(a_i\) the dollar value of the city’s amenities. Rearranging gives the value of amenities relative to other cities:
\[
a_i - a_j = (r_i - r_j) - (w_i - w_j).
\]
A city has valuable amenities if people pay more for housing than its wages justify, or accept lower wages than its housing costs require. This framework comes from Roback (1982) and is the basis of modern quality-of-life indexes.


Productivity versus quality of life
The same data reveal two different things. High wages and high housing costs mean firms value the place: it is productive. High housing costs with low wages mean households value the place: it is pleasant. Real indexes refine this with the share of income spent on housing, taxes, and the cost of other goods, but the logic is the same.

title: Measuring Quality of Life
text:
Simulation
Enter yearly wages and housing costs for two cities, and see what the model implies about how residents value their amenities.



Show the simulation code
viewof wA = Inputs.range([30000, 120000], {value: 62000, step: 500, label: "City A: average wage ($/yr)"})
viewof rA_ = Inputs.range([6000, 48000], {value: 18000, step: 250, label: "City A: housing cost ($/yr)"})
viewof wB = Inputs.range([30000, 120000], {value: 55000, step: 500, label: "City B: average wage ($/yr)"})
viewof rB = Inputs.range([6000, 48000], {value: 12000, step: 250, label: "City B: housing cost ($/yr)"})
































Show the simulation code
dA = (rA_ - rB) - (wA - wB)      // amenity value of A relative to B
Plot.plot({
  height: 220, marginLeft: 210,
  x: {label: "Dollars per year: City A minus City B →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.barX([
      {k: "Higher housing cost in A", v: rA_ - rB},
      {k: "Higher wage in A", v: wA - wB},
      {k: "Implied amenity value of A", v: dA}
    ], {x: "v", y: "k", fill: d => d.k.startsWith("Implied") ? "#881124" : "#999"})
  ]
})


















Show the simulation code
fq = d3.format(",.0f")
html`<p class="readout">Residents of City A pay $${fq(Math.abs(rA_ - rB))} ${rA_ >= rB ? "more" : "less"} for housing and earn $${fq(Math.abs(wA - wB))} ${wA >= wB ? "more" : "less"} than in City B. If both cities are in spatial equilibrium, City A's amenities are worth <strong>$${fq(Math.abs(dA))} per year ${dA >= 0 ? "more" : "less"}</strong> than City B's.</p>`


















Things to try

Set equal wages in the two cities and raise City A’s housing cost. What does the model conclude about City A?
Now give City A higher wages and higher housing costs by the same amount. Why does the model say the amenities are equal? What does the wage difference reflect instead?
Find settings where City A pays more in rent and earns less. What kind of real place looks like this?
The model assumes people can move freely. If moving is costly, which way could the estimates be wrong?

title: Measuring Quality of Life
text:
What the evidence says
Albouy (2016) uses wages, housing costs, and land values across U.S. metro areas to measure, in dollars, both how productive each place is and how much its residents value its quality of life, and then combines them into the total value of a city’s amenities. The paper turns the simple equation above into a full accounting of what places are worth. As you read, notice how it handles land values, the cost of goods other than housing, and taxes, and think about how each choice could change a city’s ranking.

title: Measuring Quality of Life
text:
Closer to home

Look up average wages and rents for Portland, Lewiston–Auburn, and Bangor. Using the simulation, which looks most “productive,” and which looks most “pleasant”?
Many people accept lower pay to live on the Maine coast. What does that suggest about its amenity value? How would you check?


Network lens: migration follows networks
The model treats every move as a free choice among cities. In practice, people move where they know people. Bailey et al. (2018) show that places linked by past migration remain socially connected for generations, and that connectedness predicts future migration. A city’s “outside option” therefore depends on who you know elsewhere, which helps explain why some places with similar wages and amenities attract very different numbers of newcomers.

title: Measuring Quality of Life
text:
Did you know?
Jennifer Roback’s 1982 framework built on work by Sherwin Rosen, who showed in 1979 that wage differences across cities could be used to value climate and other local conditions. Their combined approach, often called the Rosen–Roback model, underlies many of the “best places to live” rankings you see today, even when the rankings do not say so.
